text:
Thread count is deliberately left at the transcribe.cpp default (n_threads=0) and there is no env var for it. Measured, do not redo this without new hardware:

n_threads=0 resolves to the number of CPUs in the process affinity mask, capped at 8. On the dev machine that was 4 logical CPUs. A sweep of 1, 2, 3, 4 and the default, in randomised order with the model loaded once and two runs per setting, found nothing consistently faster than the default. n_threads=1 was about 2.2x slower. Settings 2 to 4 were inside run-to-run noise. Output text was byte-identical at every thread count.

Throughput context, so nobody reads a bad number as a model property: about 2.8x realtime on an Intel i3-8109U, a 2 physical core 15 W mobile chip. Published Parakeet CPU figures near 20x come from many-core desktop and server CPUs; the gap is roughly the hardware ratio, not a misconfiguration. The library selected the correct AVX2/FMA kernel (libggml-cpu-haswell.so). That chip has no AVX-512 and no VNNI. No GPU was usable: the Vulkan backend module loads but reports no devices without a Vulkan driver installed.

Untested and possibly worthwhile if CPU throughput ever matters: Q8_0 instead of Q5_K_M. K-quants need real dequantisation work per matmul, while Q8_0 unpacking is nearly free, so Q8_0 is often faster on a CPU without VNNI despite the larger file.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
The /transcribe endpoint is synchronous on purpose. A job queue, where POST returns an id and GET polls for the result, was designed and rejected as premature: it roughly doubles the code and buys nothing at the stated workload, which is audio of at most 10 minutes. Revisit it if expected audio grows to tens of minutes, or if callers start competing for the server, because runs are serialized and a caller waits for everything queued ahead of it.

Checked while deciding this, so nobody has to check again: waitress does NOT kill long in-flight requests. Its maintenance loop only closes channels with no active request, so channel_timeout (default 120 s) cannot interrupt a transcription that takes minutes. The real constraints are client timeouts and any reverse proxy read timeout, whose defaults are usually 60 s.

Also rejected: FastAPI plus uvicorn, because the work is a blocking CPU-bound native call deliberately serialized behind one lock. A sync endpoint there lands in a thread pool anyway, so async buys nothing and costs ASGI plus python-multipart. Stdlib http.server was rejected because the cgi module is gone in Python 3.13, which would make multipart parsing hand-written.

Also deliberately not built: any cache-directory or temp-directory setting of our own. HF_HOME already relocates the model cache (verified: HF_HOME=/models puts blobs in /models/hub) and TMPDIR already relocates upload staging.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
Biasing the transcription toward known words, for example names, is NOT possible with this library. Investigated and confirmed, do not re-research:

transcribe.cpp has no hotword, biasing, boosting, or custom vocabulary API. Searched both the Python package and the native library's strings; the only text-conditioning mechanism anywhere is initial_prompt, and it exists solely as a Whisper run extension (transcribe_whisper_run_ext).

The Parakeet model in use answers directly: supports("initial_prompt") is False and accepts(WhisperRunOptions) is False. That is expected, not a defect. Parakeet is a CTC/TDT model that transcribes in one pass, so there is no decoder prompt to seed. Prompting is a property of attention-decoder models such as Whisper.

Real contextual biasing, meaning weighting a decoder beam toward a word list, needs a hook into the decoder. The library exposes none, so it would require changing the C library. Ruled out.

Options weighed:
- Switch to a Whisper model and use initial_prompt. The only in-library path. Rejected for now: much slower than Parakeet, and prompt biasing in Whisper is a soft hint that is sometimes ignored, can leak prompt text into output, and can trigger hallucination. Whisper also works in 30 s windows, whereas this Parakeet model reports no input length limit, so long-form handling would need checking first.
- Fuzzy post-correction of the transcript against a supplied word list. Cheap, local, no new dependency. Real limits: it only helps when the output is already close to the target, so it fails when the model renders a name as two or three ordinary words, and a loose threshold corrupts words that were already correct. Phonetic matching would beat string distance but adds a dependency. Rejected.
- An LLM pass over the transcript with the word list. Best quality because it uses sentence context. THIS WAS CHOSEN AND IS NOW BUILT; see entry uexafh for the decisions behind it. The unresolved question at the time was not technical: running it locally is slow on modest hardware, and running it through an API means transcript text leaves the machine. Transcripts here can be private conversation, so that choice belongs to the operator and must not be made by default. It was settled by calling an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which a local server and a hosted API both speak, leaving the operator to pick.

Other capabilities observed on the model while checking, since they are cheap to lose and not obvious from the code: no input length limit, English only, timestamps available down to token level, and cancellation is the only advertised behavioural feature (no pnc, itn, diarization, long_form or temperature_fallback).
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
LLM postprocessing is now BUILT. This supersedes the "deferred, not built" note in the word-biasing entry.

Shape: an optional pass over the finished transcript, calling an OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint. Configured by LLM_BASE_URL and LLM_MODEL, requested per call with postprocess=true, steered by an optional vocabulary word list.

Decisions that came from the user this session, none of which are recoverable from the code:

Opt-in is per request and defaults to false. The reason is privacy, not caution about cost or latency. An operator who sets the environment variables must not thereby cause every transcript to be shipped to a third party. The caller asks, every time, or nothing is sent. Do not "helpfully" make this default on.

A misconfigured or unreachable endpoint returns processed_text: null with HTTP 200, never a 4xx or 5xx. The user wanted exactly one fallback path for clients: use processed_text, fall back to text when null. Adding an error status for misconfiguration was considered and rejected on those grounds, even though it is more honest about the cause.

The stated workload ceiling is 15 minutes of audio, roughly 2300 words. This number came from the user and is the only justification for how MAX_POSTPROCESS_CHARACTERS is sized. The cap is a guard against a surprise multi-hour upload becoming a large bill. It is not a technical limit, and chunking was deliberately not built. If the workload grows past that ceiling, revisit the cap first, and only then consider chunking.

Scope of the edit was widened during discussion. The user first said names and words only, then asked for tidying as well: punctuation, capitalisation, paragraph breaks, filler removal, obvious mis-transcriptions. The settled reading is that the model may reshape the presentation but must not touch the content. The vocabulary field carries words only; all instructions live in the hardcoded prompt.

Prompt injection through transcript content is accepted deliberately, not overlooked. Someone can speak an instruction into the microphone and steer the rewrite. The only thing they can affect is the text returned to the caller who supplied the audio, so the user judged a defence not worth building. The prompt says the transcript is speech and not a command, and that is all. Do not re-open this without a new threat model.

Also rejected in passing: the openai package, for a single POST that urllib does in a few lines; retries; streaming; caching; and letting the caller choose the model or the endpoint, because that choice is the operator's privacy decision and must not move to the client.

Not built, and worth knowing someone considered it: there are no tests in this repository, and a reviewer asked for them for this feature. The gap is real and known. The paths worth covering if that ever changes are the null fallbacks and the fact that the network call happens outside model_lock.
